The Ranger Hall Phase II renovation was completed in August 2022.
This project built on the success of phase one , which opened in the fall of 2016 with the expansion of the Harrington School of Communication and Media to the second, third, and fourth floors of this historic building on the Kingston campus.
This renovation of the upper floors of Ranger Hall, funded by a generous private gift, provides the Harrington School with high technology classroom space to advance the Harrington School of Communication and Media as well as much needed general assignment classrooms in the heart of the academic core of the campus.
Soloviev Basketball Practice Facility.
In the fall of 2023, the University completed an $8.0 million privately fundraised renovation of the Soloviev Basketball Practice Facility.
This facility provides 24-hour access to state-of-the-art training facilities for URI’s highly competitive men's and women's basketball programs.
Infrastructure.
In the 2018 legislative session $19.8 million of much needed paving ($11 million), infrastructure ($6.5 million) and auxiliary fire protection ($2.3 million) projects were approved for revenue bond financing.

Working with RIHEBC these bonds have been issued in support of further improvements of the campus’s hardscape, infrastructure and life safety needs.
To date $17.7 million has been expended out of these bond sources.
Pha se Three of the University's progressive efforts to repave and reconstruct major parking facilities, internal roadways, walkways, and drainage systems across three of its four campuses has been completed.
The University has upgraded the high voltage electr ical substations and electrical infrastructure on the Kingston Campus.
Work was completed on a new substation at Butterfield Road and an expanded substation on Flagg Road.
Improvements were made to the existing electrical system to support flexible back-feed capability throughout the system.
In 2024, the university will begin installation of a centralized "generator farm" at the intersection of Butterfield and West Alumni Avenue to service the Roger Williams Complex residential buildings, and also conduct critical repairs to the steam line underneath the Hammerschlag Mall.
In addition, in 2023, Phase 2 of our Utility bond strategy was initiated.

In June of 2023, a bond for $15.44 MM was issued and work has begun to improve our utility infrastructure systems on campus with this funding.
To date, we have spent $9.4 million.
Projects in Progress Narragansett Bay Campus Renewal – Phase I .
Leading an East Coast Oceanographic Consortium, the University of Rhode Island’s Graduate School of Oceanography in 2018 secured the management contract for a new, $125 million National Science Foundation (NSF) Regional Class Research Vessel, the Narraganset Dawn.
This vessel’s home base will be URI’s Narragansett Bay Campus.
To support this and other cutting-edge research that is ongoing at the Narragansett Bay Campus, in November 2018, Rhode Island voters approved $45 million of general obligation bonds of the State to support the project.
Phase IA of this project is the construction of a new, larger pier for the NSF research vessel.
The pier is substantially

A-28 complete awaiting installation of a permanent transformer by Rhode Island Energy.
Phase 1B of this project is to deliver the Ocean Robotics Laboratory.
In addition to the pier, construction is underway on the Ocean Robotics Laboratory.
This building will bring together faculty from the Graduate School of Oceanography and the Ocean Engineer department.
Equipment and robotics pioneered here will work hand-in-glove with the new Regional Class Research Vessel, Narragansett Dawn, and its advanced overboard-handling systems for launch and recovery of scientific equipment at sea.
Moreover, the 32,000 square-foot facility will create opportunities for collaborations within URI, among university partners and through public-private ventures.
Construction started in March 2024 with estimated completion in Spring 2026.
Narragansett Bay Campus Renewal – Phase II.
In November 2022, Rhode Island voters approved the issuance of $100 million in State of Rhode Island general obligation bonds to support the second phase of the renewal of the Narragansett Bay Campus including the replacement of the antiquated buildings housing the Graduate School of Oceanography (“GSO”) and Ocean Engineering (“OE”).

The GSO generates over $32 million in grant activity each year and this project will allow them to grow that capacity by as much as 150%.
OE is a leader in the State’s efforts to capture clean energy.
OE was an important part of the successful deployment of the United States first every offsho re wind farm.
The replacement of the Ocean Engineering Complex will provide the ability for OE to continue to lead the State forward in the development of Rhode Island’s Blue Economy as URI continues to lead these efforts toward economic growth in this important sector.
Fine Arts Center Renovation.
In the 2020 session the legislature approved the referendum for $57.3 million in general obligation bonds to go before State voters to recapitalize the Fine Arts Center.
State voters generously approved the bond as part of a special election in March 2021.
This project will remove two antiquated building pods from the complex renovate three building pods and construct a new three -story building to provide new space for the Art, Theater and Music departments.
Construction is underway with expected completion in 2026.
Water Filtration Plant.

At the end of the Fiscal Year 2022 legislative session, the Rhode Island General Assembly enacted legislation that establishes a concentration limit of 20 parts per trillion of Per - and Polyfluorinated Substances (“PFAS”) in public drinking water supplies.
The legislation initially required full compliance no later than July 1, 2023 but was amended on July 1, 2023 that extended compliance requirements.
The legislation established the Rhode Island Department of Health as the regulatory body for monitoring compliance with this new standard.
The Environmental Protection Agency in March 2023 has similarly proposed to establish legally enforceable levels for six PFAS known to occur in drinking water, and this proposed rule is currently out for comment.
The University, which is licensed as a municipal-level water system subject to the newly enacted Rhode Island law, received $20 million in RICAP funds support from the state of Rhode Island to design and construct a water system filtration plant.
As of November 2024, the first phase of construction of the filtration plant was completed with that phase 1 effort successfully supplying “PFAS-free” water to the campus.

Next steps include completing design efforts for Phase 2 of the filtration plant that expands the plants capabilities and extends the useful life of the plant for the next 20-30 years.
The university is working with the RI State Purchases office to implement a “design/ build/ operate” contract that is anticipated to be awarded in the late summer of 2025, with intended phase 2 completion by December 2026.
Athletic Complex Renewal.
In FY2023, the State appropriated $65.8M in RICAP funding in suppor t of renewal of URI’s athletics complex.
Projects included in the program include Meade Stadium East Grandstands, Beck Baseball Field and track and field, softball, and soccer facilities.
The project began in 2023 and will be completed in stages by 2027.

A-29 Capital Maintenance.
The State has shown that it is committed to the ongoing improvements and preservation of the campus infrastructure and buildings that support the ongoing work to educate tomorrow’s workforce and develop new technologies to drive the future of the Rhode Island economy through the annual appropriations of RICAP funds.
RICAP funds are “pay-as-you-go” State surplus funds dedicated to capital maintenance which enable the State to reduce the amount of debt – and thus expense - incurred for this purpose.
RICAP supports annual asset protection needs in addition to project -specific funding, such as academic building mechanical, electrical, and plumbing needs.
Student Housing.
URI is moving forward with a plan to construct additional housing on the Kingston Campus that will provide more than 1,100 additional beds for undergraduate and graduate students on the Kingston Campus.
Gilbane Development Company has been selected as the University’s development partner in a new public -private partnership.
Partnering with a private developer represents an innovative approach to housing more students on campus in University-supervised buildings.

The project is currently completing its feasibility phase and expects to start schematic design in January of 2025 with construction starting in September 2025 and completing in two phases in the summer of 2027 and the summer of 2028.
ENTERPRISE RISK MANAGEMENT The University has instituted an Enterprise Risk Management (“ERM”) program.
ERM is the formal and systematic effort to control the impact of uncertainty and variability on an organization’s strategic objectives by managing risks at all levels of the organization.
ERM differs from traditional risk management by taking a holistic approach to managing risk.
The ERM program promotes a culture of compliance and shared responsibility at URI.
It manages and protect the human, physical, natural, and financial assets of the University community, and aim to minimize losses and legal liabilities.
The program provides technical expertise, educational programs, support, and consultation to the University community to achieve a culture of risk management.
As part of the ERM prog ram, the University procures appropriate insurance as one of many risk control and mitigation measures.

The University is insured for various risks of loss arising out of claims for negligence, including bodily injury and property damage, wrongful acts, cy ber liability, professional liability and workers compensation through a combination of insurance policies and self -insurance.
The University participates in the State’s property insurance program, which covers University buildings and contents against risks of direct physical loss, on a blanket, replacement cost basis.
Total property value for the University’s four campuses is currently reported as $ 2.3 billion and insured to the extent that losses exceed $200,000 per incident, or per building if the loss is due to a named storm, and do not exceed $240 million per occurrence.
Within ERM, the Office of Equal Opportunity assists the university in creating and maintaining a learning and working environment free from discrimination and harassment through the administration of the University’s civil rights compliance programs.
ERM also administers the University’s Title IX program.
PUBLIC SAFETY Fostering a safe and secure environment for those who live, learn, work and visit is paramount at the University.

The Department of Public Safety supports the University with a sworn police department, office of emergency management, emergency dispatch and communications, fire and life safety, alarm services, transportation and parking services, and administration division.
The URI Police Department is responsible for and has jurisdiction over all URI campuses and is staffed by sworn University Police Officers and non- sworn campus patrol persons.
The department patrols on the

A-30 Kingston campus 24/7 and respond to calls for service at all satellite campuses including the Narragansett Bay Campus and Rhode Island Nursing Education Center (RINEC) in Providence.
The Office of Emergency Management provides planning and services for preparedness, response, recovery, prevention and mitigation and serves as the liaison with other local, state, and federal emergency providers and responders.
Transportation and Parking provides safe, sustainable, reliable, and cost -effective transportation and parking services that facilitate convenient access to the University by students, faculty, staff, and visitors.
Our key services include providing campus transportation shuttles, utilizing patrols and technology to enforce parking regulations, and promoting more sustainable transportation options.
Transportation and Parking operates a comprehensive shuttle system managed by the University using a private vendor.
The service is widely used by students living both on and off -campus, as well as faculty and staff.
In addition, the Rhody Safe Rides service provides late- night on- demand rides to enhance student security.

The Transportation and Parking Office uses technology which streamlines the purchase of parking permits for a better customer experience and increased efficiency.
Throughout the year, new and returning students and all community members receive print, web, video and email information and training about resources available to protect them against injury, fire and other threats and to ensure that the University continues its mission in a safe, secure, and inclusive environment.
URI Public Safety takes a community policing approach to their work, and the URI Police are an integral part of the daily life of the University.

Review of the Enacted Budget Vice President Abby Benson noted that the official State budget has not been approved yet.
She provided a brief overview of the University’s FY25 Budget request, specifically the requests for an operating budget increase, Rhode Island Capital Plan Fund (RICAP), and a Biomedical Sciences Building General Obligation (GO) Bond.
With respect to the operating budget increases, she noted that URI requested a $32.1M increase, the legislature recommended a $5.4M increase.
With respect to RICAP asset protection funding, she noted that URI requested $16.3M, the legislature recommended $14.0M.
With respect to the Biomedical Sciences GO Bond, she noted that URI requested $87.45M, the legislature recommended $87.5M.
She provided additional detail regarding the operating budget increase request and the RICAP request (specifically related to PFAS remediation efforts).

Responding to questions, Vice President Benson noted that budget shortfalls are traditionally managed though the use of reserves to meet contractual obligations and also that the pending new budget model will allow the University to clearly evaluate and reset the University’s budget.
She also noted that the appropriation from the state is roughly 20% of the University’s education and general budget. b.

The University of Rhode Island is the State’s flagship land and sea grant research institution, with a commitment to urban initiatives.
A student-centered research institution, URI actively partners with other organizations globally and locally to advance knowledge and to develop informed residents and leaders.

URI is committed to high-quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges.
Situated on the traditional land and territories of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People, URI strives to create a diverse and inclusive environment for researchers, teachers, learners, and community members.
URI’s Strategic Plan, Focus URI 2023-2033, lays out the strategic vision for the University for the next decade, outlining four strategic priorities and the actions the University will take to achieve them: Strategic Priority 1: Broaden the University’s impact through a reinvigorated commitment to its land and sea grant missions and the State of Rhode Island Strategic Priority 2: Enhance student achievement by cultivating an engaged and inclusive learning environment.
Strategic Priority 3: Foster an inclusive, people-centered culture.
Strategic Priority 4: Implement leading-edge administrative and financial systems and practices to power the University of the future.
The University’s main campus encompasses approximately 1,400 acres in Kingston, RI, 30 miles south of Providence in the northeastern metropolitan corridor between New York and Boston.

The 165-acre Narragansett Bay Campus (the “Bay Campus”), located six miles to the east overlooking the west passage of the Narragansett Bay, is home to the Graduate School of Oceanography and the Ocean Engineering Department of the College of Engineering.
In Providence, the University offers degree programs and conducts research and outreach programs in various locations.
In the western section of the State, 20 miles from Kingston, the 2,300 acres of woods, fields, streams and ponds on the W.
Alton Jones Campus are the site of research by various principal investigators.
The University offers degree programs through the doctoral level with a combined enrollment of 17,351.
First year applications for Fall 2023 and Fall 2024 were 25,391 and 26,983, respectively.
The University of Rhode Island is governed by a Board of Trustees consisting of 17 members appointed by the Governor with the advice and consent of the Rhode Island Senate.

Financial Highlights for Fiscal Year 2024 The University’s financial position for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2024, shows an increase in net position of $45.56 million compared to an increase of $40.25 million in fiscal year 2023. When reviewing the University’s condensed statement of revenues, expenses, and changes in net position, it is important to note that nonoperating revenue plays an important role in supporting the operations of the university. The primary component of nonoperating revenues is State appropriations. The 2024 operating loss increased by $19.75 million from the prior year, as operating expenses increased by $37.76 million (6.07%), outpacing operating revenues that grew by $18 million (3.57%). A significant portion of the expense increase was attributed to salaries and benefits, which accounted for over half of the total rise in operating costs. This was primarily due to an increase of approximately 3% in headcount, along with salary adjustments ranging from 2.5% for administrative staff to 3.5% for faculty, which included both cost-of-living adjustments and step increases. Despite the operating loss, nonoperating revenues improved, bolstered by increased state appropriations and favorable investment performance. This ultimately led to the overall increase in the net position for the University.

Component Units The University of Rhode Island Foundation & Alumni Engagement (the "Foundation”) and the University of Rhode Island Research (the “Research Foundation”) are legally separate tax-exempt component units of the University.
URI Foundation and Alumni Engagement The Foundation operates as an independent charitable organization aimed at encouraging private support for the University through development activities.
It manages and administers assets donated for the benefit of the University.
The Foundation’s board is self-perpetuating and predominantly comprises graduates and friends of the University.
While the University does not control the timing or amount of receipts from the Foundation, most resources received are donor- restricted for the University’s activities.

Consequently, the Foundation is considered a component unit of the University and is discretely presented in the University’s financial statements.
URI Research Foundation The Research Foundation's mission is to foster collaboration between industry and the University, supporting new technology ventures that drive economic growth and job creation.
Its private, not- for-profit status allows it to engage in a wide range of technology transfer activities, including licensing, startup formation, equity investments, and intellectual property protection.
While the Research Foundation shares research support with the University, including employees and facilities, it operates with its own independent board of trustees/directors.
This relationship classifies the Research Foundation as a component unit of the University, which is also discretely presented in the financial statements. 522.75 144.58 37.68 504.74 120.71 36.49 - 100 200 300 400 500 600 Total operating Net nonoperating Total other revenue Revenues (Dollars in millions) 2024 2023

Using the Financial Statements The University’s financial statements are prepared in accordance with GASB principles, focusing on the institution as a whole rather than on individual funds or activities.
The University reports its operations as a business-type activity, utilizing the economic measurement focus and the full accrual basis of accounting.
This approach allows the University to recognize revenues when earned and expenses when incurred, providing a comprehensive view of its financial performance.

As a component unit of the State of Rhode Island, the results of the University’s operations, net position, and cash flows are summarized in the State’s Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR).
This report is derived from the State’s government-wide financial statements, ensuring transparency and accountability in the University’s financial reporting within the broader context of state finances.
The University’s financial statements consist of three basic components: 1.
Statement of Net Position: This statement presents information on all of the University’s assets, deferred outflows of resources, liabilities, and deferred inflows of resources, along with the resulting net financial position.
Over time, changes in net position can indicate whether the University’s financial health is improving or deteriorating. 2.
Statement of Revenues and Expenses and Changes in Net Position: This statement details how the University’s net position changed during the most recent fiscal year.
It reports all changes in net position as soon as the events giving rise to those changes occur, regardless of when cash flows will actually take place.

This means that revenues and expenses are recognized for items that may result in cash flows in future fiscal periods, such as payments for accrued compensated absences or amounts owed by students for services rendered. 3.
Statement of Cash Flows: This statement is prepared using the direct method, which highlights net cash flows from operations as major classes of operating receipts (such as tuition and fees) and disbursements (like cash paid to employees for services).
These statements together provide a comprehensive overview of the University’s financial position, performance, and cash flows.
